newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Hong Kong's Tung unveils residency rights bill.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong's Tung unveils residency rights bill.

text.p: Hong Kong's post-handover leader Tung Chee-hwa on Friday unveiled a proposed law on residency rights that would maintain the status quo for most people but impose limits on those staying abroad for long periods.
Under the latest bill, permanent residents will be able to keep their status after July 1, when China regains control of the territory of 6.4 million people after 156 years of British rule.
The permanent residency issue is crucial for 750,000 Hong Kong people who have foreign citizenship but who want to know whether they can maintain their "right of abode" status after the handover.

But the law proposed by Tung would see children born in Hong Kong to non-Chinese nationals, including ethnic minorities, losing their right of abode once they reach the age of 21, forcing them to re-apply.
Chinese nationals who are Hong Kong residents would lose their right of abode only if they have declared a foreign nationality and not lived in Hong Kong for the past seven years.
Non-Chinese nationals with right of abode would lose the status if they have been out of the territory for three years.
But permanent residents who return to settle in Hong Kong within 18 months of the handover would not lose their status.
The bill says residents who lose their right of abode after the handover would still have landing rights, which do not convey the same privileges as residency rights.
The law would also allow people who have arrived in the territory illegally in the past seven years and have been allowed to stay, including Chinese dissidents, to maintain their existing status.

"For those who have illegally entered Hong Kong and obtained the Director of Immigration's authorisation to stay here before July 1 but have not yet acquired the right of abode, they may have the right of abode in the absolute discretion of the Director of Immigration as a result of the proposed amendments...after staying in Hong Kong for seven years," a statement from Tung's office said.
Those who take a similar course after handover would not have the right of abode, although they may be granted permission to stay, it said.

The bill, an amendment to the current immigration law to bring it in line with Hong Kong's post-colonial constitution, will be presented on Saturday to a Beijing-appointed interim legislature that will replace the elected Legislative Council after the handover, the statement said.
The British colonial government has repeatedly opposed the bill, warning it would invite legal challenges if it were to be handled by the interim chamber before July 1.
